chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
title: After the divorce: later Kirby recordings
summary: She didn't see him after their divorce except once around 1945, and comments on later records with tenor sax.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: After you divorced did you have much contact with him after that?

No. I didn't see Kurby after that and I'd say about 1945 I happened to be out in California and he came by the house to see me. And we talked and he was a little upset because the band, you know, he no longer had the band and evidently things weren't going as well as they might have been had the band not broken up. And so he was apparently not thinking too well. Benny Carter was living out on the west coast at the time and I think he was out there with Benny. But we didn't have much to talk about. There was no possibility of any reconciliation. We had been separated too long for that. And it was shortly after that that Kurby passed. It wasn't - I hadn't seen him any more till I heard about his death in the '50s. But I didn't even

know how well he was doing because where ever he was, you know, when you're not working together you don't hear too much about what other people are doing. And Kirby's position in the music business wasn't that popularized. I mean, he was more or less working at the better hotels. He continued to record, of course. I didn't even hear some of the later recordings of his made with other musicians because I don't know whether they were circulated or whether they was just coming or whatever, I really don't know.
Yeah, I don't know when or where that was recorded.
I think probably from the, in the period 1943 to '45, somewhere in there where he used the tenor sax instead of - in place of Russel Procope?
Yeah I noticed that. I have no idea where they might have been recorded. I never heard anything about them.
